newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CDU approves wider capital gains tax in "99.
newsitem.headline: German CDU approves wider capital gains tax in "99.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrat (CDU) party executive on Monday approved a tax reform plan which would tax capital gains on property and securities dealings from 1999 on, general secretary Peter Hintze said.
The tax plan, drawn up by CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaueble, won solid backing from party chiefs and will be put to the annual party conference later this month.
Hintze told a news conference that two amendments were made to the package, which is intended to reduce the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks and simplify Germany's labyrinthine tax system.

Taxpayers will be able to offset losses in property and securities dealings against profits in capital gains tax, Hintze said. The initial draft of Schaueble's plan foresaw assessing only capital gains.

The tax will only apply to changes in asset values which take place after the planned date of the introduction of the tax reform at the start of 1999, Hintze added, ruling out chances of passing tax reforms any earlier.
The draft also leaves open the possibility to exempt some welfare entitlements like unemployment benefits and sick pay from income tax assessments.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, leader of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), has responded to the CDU capital gains tax proposal warily, saying its impact on German financial markets needs to be assessed.
